cited_details.statement: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pretrained teacher network to provide guidance to a target student network (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).
Most existing studies manually tie intermediate features of teacher and student and transfer knowledge through predefined links (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).

Manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit distillation improvement, and identifying effective links under practical scenarios remains challenging (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).

An attention-based meta network can learn relative similarities between features and apply these similarities to control distillation intensities across all possible pairs (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).
Intermediate layers of a teacher model have been validated as effective targets for training a student to obtain better generalization (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865).
Manual association of layers can cause negative regularization from semantic mismatch between teacher-student layer pairs (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865).

An attention mechanism has been proposed to assign proper target teacher layers for each student layer, with each student layer distilling knowledge from multiple teacher layers rather than a single fixed intermediate layer (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865).

An ensemble of feature-based, response-based, and relation-based lightweight knowledge distillation has been proposed for image classification, using ResNet-20 as a student and ResNet-110 as a teacher (https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).
A large pre-trained teacher network is commonly used to train a smaller student network in knowledge distillation (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).

Student network performance degrades when the gap between student and teacher is large, and a teacher can effectively transfer its knowledge to students only up to a certain size (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).
Multi-step knowledge distillation employs an intermediate-sized network, called a teacher assistant, to bridge the gap between the student and teacher (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).
Most existing distillation approaches apply a fixed pre-trained model in teacher-student learning, motivating evolutionary approaches to student network design (https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13811).

Knowledge distillation is widely used to transfer knowledge from one network to another, but dependence on accompanying assistive models complicates training and adds large memory and time cost (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).

A self-distillation mechanism has been designed to transfer knowledge between different distorted versions of the same training data without reliance on accompanying models (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).

Learning consistent global feature distributions and posterior class probabilities across distorted data versions has improved generalization on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet for AlexNet, ResNet, Wide ResNet, and DenseNet (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).

Offline distillation methods rely on a strong pre-trained teacher, enabling favorable knowledge discovery and transfer but requiring a complex two-phase training procedure (https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).
Online counterparts address this two-phase training limitation at the price of lacking a high-capacity teacher (https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).

An On-the-fly Native Ensemble strategy trains a single multi-branch network while simultaneously establishing a strong teacher on the fly to enhance the learning of the target network (https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).

Deep learning models achieve success across many fields but are huge in size, with millions or billions of parameters, and cannot be deployed on systems with limited resources such as embedded systems and mobile phones (https://doi.org/10.3390/math8101652).
Some work has focused on the architecture of the student as the receiver of dark knowledge, searching for better students to learn distilled knowledge (https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.11612).
Data-efficient distillation from a black-box model has been studied using active mixup, with neural networks shown to be more productive teachers than human raters (https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.13960).
A framework has been proposed to learn student-friendly teacher networks for knowledge distillation (http://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07650).
Deep neural networks achieve appealing results on many tasks but are too large to deploy on edge devices like smartphones or embedded sensor nodes (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v34i04.5963).
Manual selection of feature links limits the improvement achievable from distillation (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i9.16969).
Semantic mismatch between teacher-student layer pairs can cause negative regularization when layers are manually associated (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v35i8.16865).

Offline distillation requires a strong pre-trained teacher and a complex two-phase training procedure, while online counterparts lack a high-capacity teacher (https://qmro.qmul.ac.uk/xmlui/handle/123456789/58358).
Self-distillation avoids accompanying teacher models but still faces the practical cost of large memory and time requirements (https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33015565).
